extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys and practitioners handling PTAB IPR/CBM/PGR proceedings and related Federal Circuit/Supreme Court appeals
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes procedural and substantive legal standards, burdens, evidentiary rules, and appellate review principles that govern USPTO post‑grant proceedings (IPR/CBM/PGR) and related Federal Circuit/Supreme Court decisions. Useful for practitioners evaluating petitions, responding to PTAB actions, or litigating appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petitioner’s burden of proof in AIA proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The petitioner’s burden of evidentiary proof in AIA post‑grant proceedings is “by a preponderance of the evidence.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This differs from the district court standard of “clear and convincing evidence,” and contributes to the perception that patents are easier to invalidate in PTAB proceedings than in district court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of judicial review for PTAB decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency conclusions of law are reviewed de novo, while findings of fact are reviewed for substantial evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Microsoft/Proxyconn and related decisions confirm the two-track review standard: legal questions receive de novo review; factual findings receive substantial‑evidence review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appealability of PTAB institution decisions (general rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Cuozzo and 35 U.S.C. § 314(d), a PTAB determination whether to institute inter partes review is generally final and nonappealable after a final written decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cuozzo held institution decisions are not appealable after final written decision; however, that general rule has limited carveouts discussed elsewhere (see timeliness appeals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appealability of timeliness determinations (§315(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal Circuit en banc in Wi‑Fi One held PTAB determinations that IPR petitions are timely filed (satisfaction of §315(b)) are appealable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court cited the strong presumption in favor of judicial review and found no clear congressional intent to bar review of timeliness determinations; this overruled earlier contrary case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing required to appeal PTAB decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: An appellant seeking judicial review of a PTAB final action must establish Article III standing: (1) injury in fact that is concrete and particularized, (2) causation (fairly traceable), and (3) redressability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phigenix illustrates lack of standing when petitioner failed to allege risk of infringement, licensor/licensing status, or prospective activity implicating the patent; courts may exclude parties lacking such proof. Separate parties who prevailed before the PTAB may nevertheless appear to defend the decision if the appellant has Article III standing (Personal Audio).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignor estoppel and §314(d) nonreviewability
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have held they lack jurisdiction to review PTAB determinations that assignor estoppel does not preclude institution of an IPR because §314(d) bars review of institution decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Husky demonstrates that arguments about equitable doctrines affecting institution (assignor estoppel) can be nonreviewable under §314(d), absent issues implicating constitutional questions or statutes reaching beyond §314(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice and opportunity to respond under the APA
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA requires the PTAB to timely inform the patent owner of the matters of fact and law asserted and to give interested parties an opportunity to submit and consider facts and arguments, including rebuttal evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to provide adequate notice or an opportunity to respond (e.g., relying heavily on material first cited in a petitioner’s reply) can violate the APA and lead to vacatur/remand (NuVasive, EmeraChem). Specificity in petitions and institution decisions matters: detailed claim charts and identified passages constrain what the patent owner can be fairly expected to address.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of new material in reply and right to respond
rubrics_metrics.description: When petitioner or the PTAB relies on material not previously presented (e.g., a passage cited in a reply), the patent owner must be given an adequate opportunity to respond; otherwise reliance on that material in the final decision may violate the APA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NuVasive: denial of motions to strike or surreplies and refusal to address the new material at hearing led to vacatur/remand because the PTAB treated the newly cited material as essential to its obviousness findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of persuasion for amended/substitute claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Circuit in Aqua Products (en banc) concluded the most reasonable reading of 35 U.S.C. §316(e) places the burden of persuasion regarding patentability of amended claims on the petitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PTAB erred when it imposed the burden of proving patentability of proposed substitute claims on the patent owner; Aqua raised questions about permissible burdens (persuasion vs production) and Chevron deference to PTO interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petitioner must show substitute claims are unpatentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Consistent with Aqua Products' guidance, the petitioner bears the burden of demonstrating that proposed substitute claims are unpatentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This affects motion‑to‑amend practice and how PTAB should allocate burdens when patent owners propose substitutes under §316(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: PTAB evidentiary rulings and supplemental evidence (37 C.F.R. § 42.123(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Requests to submit new information must show (1) why the supplemental information reasonably could not have been obtained earlier, and (2) that consideration of the supplemental information would be in the interests of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ultratec: the Federal Circuit found the patentee satisfied those requirements and that the PTAB abused its discretion by refusing to admit supplemental evidence (expert trial testimony). Agencies must explain basis for excluding material evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary exclusions must be justified; hearsay and authentication issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Excluding exhibits for hearsay or lack of authentication requires correct legal analysis; material communications by the patentee may be probative (e.g., an email showing conception).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: REG Synthetic Fuels: the court reversed PTAB hearsay exclusion where an email was probative of conception. PTAB must provide reasoned basis for evidentiary exclusions and consider legal significance of documentary evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTAB decisions must provide sufficient explanation and support
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTAB must disclose clear, adequately sustained grounds and reasoning underlying its determinations so that courts can perform meaningful review under Chenery and related precedents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PersonalWeb and Shinn Fu emphasize that the amount of explanation required depends on context: more complex or obscure technologies or nonobvious prior‑art combinations demand more detailed analysis. Failure to explain why references disclose claim elements or why a skilled artisan would be motivated to combine them can lead to vacatur/remand.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTAB obligation to address parties’ arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTAB has an obligation to address the substantive arguments presented by the parties; it cannot ignore or fail to analyze key combinations or contentions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shinn Fu: PTAB granted motion to amend and then failed to analyze the petitioner’s obviousness combination in its final written decision, making meaningful review impossible and rendering the decision arbitrary and capricious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction standard — broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Cuozzo the USPTO may use the broadest reasonable interpretation for claim construction in PTAB proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BRI remains permissible at the PTAB, but the PTAB must still reach reasonable constructions in light of the specification; simple reliance on dictionary definitions without context may not result in the broadest reasonable interpretation (PPC Broadband).

rubrics_metrics.name: Means‑plus‑function claim construction requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: When construing means‑plus‑function limitations, the PTAB must identify the claimed function and the corresponding structure, material, or acts in the specification that perform that function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IPcom required the PTAB to identify the corresponding algorithm or structure even when applying BRI; failure to do so requires vacatur and remand for proper construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTAB may reach different results than district courts due to record and burden differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Different records and different burdens of proof (preponderance at PTAB vs clear and convincing in district court) mean PTAB outcomes may differ from district court findings and such divergence is not per se improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novartis: courts recognized it is unsurprising that different records may lead to different conclusions; USPTO ideally should not arrive at a different conclusion on identical evidence, but it is not an absolute rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statements made during IPR can create prosecution disclaimer
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent owner statements during IPR proceedings (pre‑ or post‑institution) can be used to support claim constructions under the doctrine of prosecution disclaimer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aylus: a patent owner’s preliminary response asserting a limiting interpretation was deemed a “clear and unmistakable” disavowal relied upon during later claim construction in district court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mootness of subsequent appeals after invalidation
rubrics_metrics.description: Once claims are invalidated in one post‑grant proceeding, certain other challenges to the same claims may be moot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unwired Planet: the Federal Circuit dismissed as moot an appeal of a CBM decision after those same claims had been invalidated in an IPR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of judicial review of agency action
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a strong presumption in favor of judicial review of agency actions; Congress must clearly and convincingly indicate an intent to prohibit review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wi‑Fi One relied on this presumption in holding timeliness determinations appealable; it is a key interpretive principle when assessing whether particular PTAB decisions are reviewable.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTAB must not change theories in midstream without notice
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTAB should not adopt new theories, claim constructions, or factual bases in its final written decision in a way that deprives parties of notice and an opportunity to respond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SAS, Dell, and other cases stress that changing theories midstream or relying on factual assertions introduced only at oral argument can deny parties procedural rights and lead to reversal/vacatur.

rubrics_metrics.name: §318(a) statutory question — whether PTAB must decide every challenged claim
rubrics_metrics.description: A pending Supreme Court question (SAS) asked whether 35 U.S.C. § 318(a) requires the PTAB to issue a final written decision addressing the patentability of every claim challenged by the petitioner, or whether partial decisions are permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The outcome affects institution and final decision practice; practitioners should monitor case law for the resolution of the statutory interpretation issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTAB institution and motion-to-amend denials can be subject to review for arbitrary and capricious action
rubrics_metrics.description: Denials of motions to amend or other agency rulings that lack reasoned explanation may be found arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act and set aside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Veritas/Idle Free and Aqua Products’ related proceedings illustrate judicial scrutiny when the PTAB’s treatment of motions to amend appears unexplained or inconsistent with statutory requirements.
